items.value: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Deuskar's 'desh' meant the whole country, not Bengal alone
items.reasoning: Desher Katha (1904) attacked colonial rule for more than its economic drain: it warned that the deeper conquest was of the Indian mind, which the colonial state had cast a spell over, so statement 1 holds. The book's extraordinary popularity fed straight into the swadeshi repertoire of street plays, jatra and folk song, so statement 2 holds. Statement 3 is what settles the option: Deuskar was a Marathi-descended writer working in Bengali, and his 'desh' was the whole country whose exploitation he documented, not the region of Bengal. Since statement 3 appears in every other option, only A survives.

items.value: The Pact included 1, 2 and 4; the demand for an inquiry into police excesses was refused
items.reasoning: Under the pact of March 1931 the Government undertook to withdraw the ordinances issued to suppress the Civil Disobedience Movement and to release political prisoners other than those convicted of violence, while the Congress agreed to suspend the movement and to attend the second Round Table Conference - statements 1, 2 and 4. Gandhi's demand for a public inquiry into police excesses was the one substantial point Irwin refused, so statement 3 is wrong and options C and D fall with it.

items.value: Vital-Vidhvansak was published by Gopal Baba Walangkar
items.reasoning: Gopal Baba Walangkar, a retired army man of the Mahar community and an early follower of the Satyashodhak tradition, began Vital-Vidhvansak in 1888, and it is regarded as the first periodical addressed to untouchable readers. Phule's own journal was Deenbandhu, and Ambedkar's first paper, Mooknayak, appeared only in 1920, three decades later.

items.value: Kulyavapa and dronavapa are units of land measurement
items.reasoning: Kulyavapa, dronavapa and adhavapa occur in the Gupta-period copper-plate land grants of Bengal. Each expresses area indirectly, as the extent of land that a given measure of seed - a kulya, a drona - would sow, so the terms belong to land measurement and not to coinage, to categories of urban land or to ritual.

items.value: The inscription is Ashoka's
items.reasoning: The passage is from Ashoka's Rock Edict XII, on concord among religious sects. He urges restraint both in praising one's own sect and in disparaging others, warning that immoderate devotion injures the very sect it means to glorify. This plea for samavaya among sects is a hallmark of Ashoka's dhamma and is not associated with any of the other rulers named.

items.value: Paramitas are the perfections whose attainment leads along the Bodhisattva path
items.reasoning: In Mahayana thought the paramitas are the perfections a Bodhisattva cultivates - in the standard list of six, generosity, moral conduct, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom - and it is their perfection that carries him along the Bodhisattva path towards Buddhahood. The aphoristic law texts are the Dharmasutras, the schools rejecting Vedic authority are the nastika systems, and the great South Indian merchant guilds were the Ayyavole and the Manigramam.

items.value: The Rakhmabai case involved all three - women's education, the age of consent, and restitution of conjugal rights
items.reasoning: Rakhmabai, married as a child and then educated in her stepfather's household, refused to join her husband; Dadaji's suit of 1884 was in terms a suit for restitution of conjugal rights, which is statement 3 and the literal subject of the litigation. Because she had been married before she was old enough to consent, the case became the leading argument for raising the age of consent and fed directly into the Age of Consent Act of 1891, which is statement 2. Statement 1 is the judgement call: her schooling was itself part of the controversy, being blamed for her defiance, and her own letters to the press signed 'A Hindu Lady' pressed the case for educating girls instead of despatching them to their husbands. Option B, reading the case narrowly as consent plus restitution, is the runner-up.

items.value: Indigo declined because synthetic dye made natural indigo unprofitable in the world market
items.reasoning: Natural indigo was destroyed by chemistry rather than by politics. Adolf von Baeyer's synthesis of indigo was commercialised by BASF from 1897, and within a decade the cheap synthetic dye had swept the world market, leaving Indian plantations unable to compete. Peasant resistance had ended indigo in Bengal much earlier and only locally, and it cannot explain the collapse of the trade as a whole by the beginning of the twentieth century.

items.value: Fort William College was founded to train British civil servants for administration in India
items.reasoning: Wellesley set up Fort William College in 1800 because the young writers arriving from England reached India knowing nothing of its languages, laws or customs; the College taught them Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit and the vernaculars before they took up office. A revival of oriental learning and employment for scholars such as William Carey were by-products, not the purpose, and Wellesley acted on his own initiative - the Court of Directors in fact disapproved and reduced the institution.

items.value: Ulgulan describes Birsa Munda's revolt of 1899-1900
items.reasoning: Ulgulan, the Great Tumult, is the name given to the Munda rising led by Birsa Munda in Chotanagpur in 1899-1900 against the dikus, the landlords and the colonial revenue and forest system, in which Birsa also preached a new faith to his followers. The Revolt of 1857, the Mappila Rebellion and the Indigo Revolt are all known by other names.

items.value: Only statement 3 is correct - Kalidasa is associated with Chandragupta II
items.reasoning: Kalidasa is placed by tradition among the nine gems of the court of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, so statement 3 is correct. Panini, the grammarian of the Ashtadhyayi, lived several centuries before the Shungas; the scholar linked with Pushyamitra Shunga is Patanjali, whose Mahabhashya is a commentary on Panini, so statement 1 confuses the two. Amarasimha, who compiled the Amarakosha, is likewise counted among Chandragupta II's gems and not among the literary men of Harshavardhana's court, who were Banabhatta and Mayura, so statement 2 is wrong.

items.value: Pronuclear transfer is used to prevent mitochondrial diseases in offspring
items.reasoning: Pronuclear transfer is a mitochondrial replacement technique. The mother's egg is fertilised, and the two pronuclei are then lifted out of the resulting zygote and placed in a donor zygote whose own pronuclei have been removed but whose mitochondria are healthy. The nuclear DNA remains the parents' and only the mitochondria are the donor's, so a mother carrying a mitochondrial disorder can avoid transmitting it to her child.

items.value: Artificial Intelligence can do 1, 3 and 4 - cut industrial electricity use, diagnose disease and convert text to speech - but not transmit electrical energy wirelessly
items.reasoning: Statement 5 settles the item: transmitting electrical energy without wires is a problem of physics and engineering - resonant inductive coupling, microwave or laser power beaming - and is not something an algorithm performs, so every option containing it falls and only B survives. Of the rest, AI schedules and optimises industrial and data-centre energy use (1), reads medical images and clinical data to support diagnosis (3), and drives modern text-to-speech systems (4). Statement 2 is defensible on its own terms, since generative models do produce stories and songs; the printed options offer no combination of 1, 2, 3 and 4, so the item only resolves if 'meaningful' is read strictly.

items.value: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct; VLC is short-range, not long-range
items.reasoning: Statement 2 decides the item and appears in every option except C: visible light communication depends on line of sight and on light that does not travel far, so it is a short-range optical wireless technology and calling it long-range is wrong. The others hold - VLC works in the visible band of roughly 375 to 780 nanometres (1), reaches data rates far above Bluetooth's (3), and because it carries data on light rather than on radio waves it neither causes nor suffers radio-frequency interference, which is why it can be used in hospitals, aircraft and other electromagnetically sensitive places (4).

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; a blockchain is not limited to cryptocurrency data
items.reasoning: A public blockchain is a shared, append-only ledger that any participant can inspect and verify and that no single party owns or administers, which is statement 1. It is permissionless in the further sense that anyone may build an application on it without seeking approval from an operator, which is statement 3. Statement 2 is wrong: the ledger is indifferent to what it records, and supply-chain events, land records, identity attestations and smart contracts all sit on blockchains - cryptocurrency is simply the first and best-known application.

items.value: All four are correct - carbon nanotubes carry drugs and antigens, can form artificial capillaries, work in biochemical sensors, and are biodegradable
items.reasoning: Nanotubes are studied as vehicles for delivering drugs and antigens into the body (1), and their conductivity and enormous surface-to-volume ratio make them sensitive transducers in biochemical sensors (3), so any option omitting these fails and only C and D remain. Statement 4 is not the older textbook position but is supported by the finding that nanotubes are degraded enzymatically, for instance by neutrophil myeloperoxidase, and both surviving options require it. Statement 2 is the judgement call - nanotube scaffolds have been explored as artificial capillaries and vascular grafts for injured tissue - and accepting it gives all four; rejecting it would give option C, the runner-up.

items.value: Drones can do all three - spray pesticides, inspect volcanic craters, and collect whale breath samples
items.reasoning: All three are done with current technology. Agricultural drones spray pesticide over crop fields and are in routine commercial use. Drones are flown over and into volcanic craters to sample gases and image vents where a crewed aircraft could not safely go. And drones of the SnotBot type hover in the blow of a surfacing whale to catch the exhaled spray, from which DNA, hormones and microbiota are analysed without ever touching the animal.

items.value: The experiment is Evolved LISA (eLISA)
items.reasoning: Three spacecraft flying in an equilateral formation with arms a million kilometres long and laser links between them is the design of the space-based gravitational-wave observatory in the LISA family, and the one-million-kilometre arm belongs to the Evolved LISA configuration. LISA Pathfinder was a single spacecraft flown only to test the instrument technology, so it cannot be the trio described, and Voyager-2 and New Horizons are single planetary probes.

items.value: All three are correct - germline cells can be edited, an embryo's genome can be edited before birth, and human iPSCs can be injected into a pig embryo
items.reasoning: All three are within reach of current technique. Editing can be directed at the germline cells that give rise to eggs and sperm, so that the change is heritable (1). An embryo's genome can be edited at the one-cell or early cleavage stage, which is what was done in the CRISPR-edited human embryos reported in 2018 (2). And human induced pluripotent stem cells have been injected into pig embryos to create human-pig chimaeras in research aimed at growing transplantable organs (3).

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; the claim that the vaccines have no side effects is false
items.reasoning: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes not only pneumonia but also meningitis, bacteraemia and sepsis, and the conjugate vaccine protects against the serotypes responsible for all of these, so statement 1 holds. Preventing the infection means the antibiotic is never needed, which cuts both antibiotic consumption and the selection pressure that breeds resistant strains, so statement 2 holds. Statement 3 is wrong on its face - no vaccine is free of side effects, and PCV commonly causes injection-site pain, swelling and fever and can rarely provoke allergic reactions.

items.value: Public Key Infrastructure belongs to digital security infrastructure
items.reasoning: Public Key Infrastructure is the framework of public and private key pairs, digital certificates, Certifying Authorities and the Controller of Certifying Authorities that underpins digital signatures and encrypted communication; in India it rests on the Information Technology Act, 2000. The term belongs to information security and has nothing to do with food, health, education, telecommunication or transport infrastructure.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; plant cells do have a plasma membrane, so statement 2 is false
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is false and that alone fixes the answer: a plant cell has a plasma membrane exactly as an animal cell does, and the cellulose wall lies outside that membrane rather than replacing it. Statement 1 states the real difference, the wall of cellulose that animal cells lack. Statement 3 states the other standard difference - a mature plant cell is dominated by a single large central vacuole, whereas an animal cell has only small and scattered vacuoles and vesicles.

items.value: All five are routes of benzene exposure
items.reasoning: Benzene reaches people mainly by inhalation and all the listed routes carry it. It is a constituent of petrol and appears in vehicle exhaust (1); tobacco smoke is the largest single source of exposure for smokers and a major indoor source for others (2); the incomplete combustion of wood and other biomass releases it (3); and it occurs in the solvents of paints, lacquers, varnishes, glues and furniture wax, so freshly varnished furniture off-gasses it indoors (4). Statement 5 is the weakest link - benzene is a feedstock for plastics and resins, and polyurethane products can off-gas volatile organic compounds including benzene. Once statement 4 is accepted the printed options leave only 'all of the above', since options B and C omit statements that are certainly true; option A, which would follow if both 4 and 5 were rejected, is the runner-up.

items.value: Only not depending on short-term foreign borrowings would give India immunity
items.reasoning: Short-term foreign borrowing is the classic vulnerability in a crisis, because it must be rolled over at exactly the moment foreign lenders are withdrawing, so a country that has kept it small is far less exposed to a sudden stop - statement 1 is protective. The other two work the other way. Admitting more foreign banks multiplies the channels through which a shock abroad is transmitted to the domestic system, as a parent bank in difficulty pulls funds home. And full capital account convertibility removes precisely the friction that slows a stampede of capital out of the country; India's only partial convertibility was widely credited with insulating it in 2008.

items.value: The aggregate money supply is left unchanged
items.reasoning: Money supply on the M1 measure is currency held by the public plus demand deposits with banks plus other deposits with the Reserve Bank. Withdrawing cash simply moves rupees between the first two components: demand deposits fall by the amount withdrawn and currency with the public rises by exactly the same amount, so the total is unchanged and the immediate effect is nil. What does change is the banking system's reserves, which can affect the credit the banks create later - but that is a second-round effect, not the immediate one the question asks about.
